reference.source: Mulliken and Young's Vascular Anomalies: Hemangiomas and Malformations
clinicalPearls: Slow-flow malformation of dysplastic venous channels present at birth, though sometimes only apparent later; grows proportionately and does not involute.
Soft, compressible, blue-purple lesion that swells with dependency, Valsalva or crying and empties on compression or elevation.
Phleboliths (calcified thrombi) are pathognomonic and a common cause of localised pain.
Sporadic lesions commonly harbour somatic TIE2 (TEK) mutations; PIK3CA mutations also occur, and familial mucocutaneous forms are TEK-related.
Localised intravascular coagulopathy with raised D-dimer and low fibrinogen is common and can worsen with intervention or in extensive lesions.
Sclerotherapy is first-line for most symptomatic lesions; surgery is reserved for well-localised disease.
Glomuvenous malformations (glomulin gene) are firmer, more nodular and painful on compression, forming a distinct subtype.
MRI best characterises extent, while ultrasound shows compressible channels with slow or absent flow.
reference.pathophysiology: Venous malformation is a congenital slow-flow vascular malformation composed of ectatic, thin-walled venous channels lined by flat, quiescent endothelium with a deficient and irregular smooth-muscle layer, which impairs contraction and causes progressive dilatation and stasis. Most sporadic lesions arise from somatic activating mutations in the endothelial receptor TIE2 (TEK) or in PIK3CA, driving PI3K/AKT/mTOR signalling. Venous stasis within the malformation activates coagulation locally, producing a chronic localised intravascular coagulopathy with thrombosis, phlebolith formation and pain.
additionalDifferentials: Soft-tissue tumour such as a haemangiopericytoma
additionalInvestigations: Doppler ultrasound showing compressible channels with monophasic slow or absent flow
Contrast-enhanced MRI (T2-hyperintense lobulated lesion with phleboliths)
Coagulation screen including D-dimer and fibrinogen
Direct phlebography at the time of sclerotherapy
Genetic testing (TEK, PIK3CA) in selected or familial cases
redFlags: Rapid painful swelling suggesting acute thrombosis
Extensive lesions with severe localised intravascular coagulopathy risking haemorrhage
reference.prognosis: Venous malformations are chronic and tend to enlarge slowly over life, particularly around puberty. Symptoms are often controllable with sclerotherapy and compression, but complete cure is uncommon in extensive lesions.
pitfalls: Using the obsolete term cavernous haemangioma and implying that the lesion will involute.
Neglecting to assess and correct localised intravascular coagulopathy before intervention.
Mistaking phlebolith pain for another cause.
Assuming surgery alone will cure a diffuse lesion.
references: Consensus guidance on diagnosis and management of venous malformations
management: Offer sclerotherapy as first-line treatment for most symptomatic lesions, reserving surgical resection for well-localised disease
Consider the mTOR inhibitor sirolimus for extensive or complex malformations not amenable to sclerotherapy or surgery
Provide conservative measures including graduated compression garments, analgesia and aspirin for pain from localised intravascular coagulopathy and phleboliths
Monitor and manage the localised intravascular coagulopathy with D-dimer and fibrinogen, giving low-molecular-weight heparin around procedures in extensive lesions
Consider targeted therapy directed at PIK3CA in selected genetically defined cases
Manage through a multidisciplinary vascular anomalies team with long-term follow-up, as lesions enlarge around puberty and are rarely cured when extensive
